facts.statement: The extinct genus Tsoabichi means "monster" in the Shoshone language and belongs to the caimanine crocodylians.
facts.quote: Tsoabichi (from Shoshone "tso'abichi'", meaning "monster") is an extinct genus of caimanine crocodylian.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Christopher A. Brochu named and described the genus Tsoabichi in 2010, designating Tsoabichi greenriverensis as the type species.
facts.quote: The genus was named and described in 2010 by paleontologist Christopher A. Brochu, with the type species being Tsoabichi greenriverensis.

facts.statement: Fossils of Tsoabichi come from the Green River Formation in Wyoming and date to the Ypresian stage of the Eocene.
facts.quote: Fossils are known from the Green River Formation in Wyoming, and date back to the Ypresian stage of the Eocene (Wasatchian stage of North American age).

facts.statement: Unlike some living caimans, Tsoabichi lacked a bony ridge between the eyes but possessed three smaller ridges between the eye sockets.
facts.quote: Tsoabichi lacks a spectacle, but it does have three smaller ridges between the orbits, or eye sockets.

facts.statement: The supraoccipital bone on the Tsoabichi skull table formed a distinct V-shape.
facts.quote: Much of the supraoccipital bone is also found on the skull table, and forms a V-shape.

facts.statement: Tsoabichi had wider dorsal osteoderms than other caimans, and some of these bony scutes featured two keels on their outer surface.
facts.quote: The dorsal osteoderms (bony scutes along the back) are wider than those of other caimans. Some have two keels on their outer surface.

facts.statement: Tsoabichi possessed bipartite ventral osteoderms on its underside.
facts.quote: Tsoabichi also has bipartite ventral osteoderms on its underside.

facts.statement: Tsoabichi is one of the few known caimanines that lived north of modern-day Mexico, whereas most caimans are found in Central and South America.
facts.quote: Tsoabichi is one of the few caimanines known to have lived north of what is now Mexico; the majority of caimans living and extinct are known from Central and South America.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Tsoabichi originated in North America or South America, though researchers suggest it likely came from a South American population that reentered North America in the Early Eocene.
facts.quote: Tsoabichi most likely originated from a South American population that reentered North America in the Early Eocene.

facts.statement: Tsoabichi lived during the Ypresian stage, approximately 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Brochu (2010) found it to be a basal member of Caimaninae closely related to the living genus Paleosuchus.

rejected.quote: The analysis of Hastings et al. (2013), which included several more species of caimans, also placed Tsoabichi in a basal position within Caimaninae as the sister taxon to crown group caimans.
